_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.point: First conjugation present tense (-are verbs)
entries.label: Present (1st conj.)
entries.usage: The amō family now: -ō, -ās, -at on the a-stem.
entries.example: Puella puerum amat. — The girl loves the boy.

entries.point: Second conjugation present tense (-ere verbs with -e-)
entries.label: Present (2nd conj.)
entries.usage: The videō/habeō family: the -e- stays visible before every ending.
entries.example: Puer puellam videt. — The boy sees the girl.

entries.point: Third and fourth conjugation present (dico, audio)
entries.label: Present (3rd/4th conj.)
entries.usage: Short changeable vowel (dīcit, dīcunt) or steady -i- (audit, audiunt).
entries.example: Puella verbum dīcit. — The girl says a word.

entries.point: sum, esse — the irregular verb "to be"
entries.label: sum (to be)
entries.usage: The irregular linker: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt.
entries.example: Puella bona est. — The girl is good.

entries.point: possum, posse — "to be able" with an infinitive
entries.label: possum (can)
entries.usage: pot- + sum says what someone can do, with an infinitive.
entries.example: Puella aquam vidēre potest. — The girl can see the water.

entries.point: Imperfect tense (-bam): what used to happen
entries.label: Imperfect
entries.usage: Ongoing or repeated past — the -ba- signature in every conjugation.
entries.example: Dominus bonus erat. — The master was good.

entries.point: Future tense (-bo/-bis and -am/-es)
entries.label: Future
entries.usage: What will happen: -bō/-bis in conjugations 1-2, -am/-ēs in 3-4.
entries.example: Bellum magnum erit. — The war will be great.

entries.point: Perfect tense: amavi, vidi, dixi
entries.label: Perfect
entries.usage: Done and reported: perfect stem + -ī, -istī, -it.
entries.example: Rēgīna rēgem amāvit. — The queen loved the king.

entries.point: Pluperfect tense: amaveram "I had loved"
entries.label: Pluperfect
entries.usage: Past before the past: perfect stem + -eram.
entries.example: Rēx verba dīxerat. — The king had said the words.

entries.point: Imperatives: giving commands
entries.label: Commands
entries.usage: Bare stem for one person, -te for several: amā!, amāte!
entries.example: Portā aquam, puer! — Carry the water, boy!

entries.point: Present passive: amatur "is loved"
entries.label: Present passive
entries.usage: The subject receives the action: -tur, -ntur, agent with ā/ab.
entries.example: Puella ā puerō amātur. — The girl is loved by the boy.

entries.point: Perfect passive participle and perfect passive
entries.label: Perfect passive
entries.usage: Participle + est says what was done: capta est, audīta sunt.
entries.example: Urbs capta est. — The city was captured.

entries.point: The subjunctive mood: present and imperfect forms
entries.label: Subjunctive
entries.usage: Wishes and let-us forms: the conjugation vowel swaps (amet, videat).
entries.example: Vīvat rēx! — Long live the king!

entries.point: Deponent verbs: loquor, sequor
entries.label: Deponents
entries.usage: Passive endings, active meaning: loquitur = she speaks.
entries.example: Puella cum puerō loquitur. — The girl speaks with the boy.

entries.point: Gerund, gerundive, and the passive periphrastic
entries.label: Gerund & gerundive
entries.usage: Naming the activity itself (ars amandī) and saying what has to be done: dēlenda est.
entries.example: Carthāgō dēlenda est. — Carthage must be destroyed.

entries.point: Nominative and accusative: subject and direct object
entries.label: Subject vs object
entries.usage: The ending, not the position, says who acts and who is acted on.
entries.example: Puella puerum videt. — The girl sees the boy.

entries.point: First declension nouns: -a / -ae feminine
entries.label: 1st declension
entries.usage: The puella pattern: -a, genitive -ae, accusative -am.
entries.example: Nōmen puellae est Iūlia. — The girl's name is Julia.

entries.point: Second declension nouns: -us masculine and -um neuter
entries.label: 2nd declension
entries.usage: The dominus and bellum patterns; neuters keep one form for subject and object.
entries.example: Dominus bonus est. — The master is good.

entries.point: Third declension nouns: rex, regis and urbs, urbis
entries.label: 3rd declension
entries.usage: Unpredictable nominatives, reliable stem endings: rēgem, rēgis, rēge.
entries.example: Puella rēgem in urbe videt. — The girl sees the king in the city.

entries.point: Third declension neuters: corpus, tempus, nomen
entries.label: 3rd decl. neuters
entries.usage: Corpus, tempus, nōmen: subject and object match, plural in -a.
entries.example: Corpora magna sunt. — The bodies are big.

entries.point: Fourth and fifth declension: manus and dies
entries.label: 4th/5th declension
entries.usage: The small -u- and -e- families: manus, diēs, rēs.
entries.example: Diēs longus est. — The day is long.

entries.point: Genitive and dative at work
entries.label: Genitive & dative
entries.usage: Whose it is (rēgis) and to whom it goes (puellae, puerō).
entries.example: Puer puellae aquam dat. — The boy gives water to the girl.

entries.point: Adjective-noun agreement
entries.label: Agreement
entries.usage: The adjective copies its noun's gender, number, and case.
entries.example: Puella magna est. — The girl is big.

entries.point: Comparison of adjectives: altior, altissimus
entries.label: Comparison
entries.usage: Taller and tallest: -ior for the comparative, -issimus for the superlative.
entries.example: Rēx fortissimus est. — The king is very brave.

entries.point: Personal pronouns: ego, tu, nos, vos
entries.label: Pronouns
entries.usage: Ego and tū for emphasis; mē, tē, nōs, vōs as objects.
entries.example: Ego tē amō. — I love you.

entries.point: Demonstratives: hic "this" and ille "that"
entries.label: hic & ille
entries.usage: This-here and that-there, agreeing like adjectives: hunc, hanc, illam.
entries.example: Haec puella bona est. — This girl is good.

entries.point: Prepositions: in + accusative vs. in + ablative
entries.label: in + case
entries.usage: Accusative for motion into, ablative for sitting in or on.
entries.example: Puella in īnsulā habitat. — The girl lives on the island.

entries.point: Word order: Latin puts case marking to work
entries.label: Word order
entries.usage: Endings free the order — subject-object-verb is only the neutral default.
entries.example: Puerum puella amat. — The girl loves the boy. (object fronted)

entries.point: Questions: -ne, quis and quid
entries.label: Questions
entries.usage: Yes/no with the -ne particle; quis and quid ask who and what.
entries.example: Vidēsne puellam? — Do you see the girl?

entries.point: Relative clauses: qui, quae, quod
entries.label: Relative qui
entries.usage: Who/which clauses: gender from the noun, case from the job inside.
entries.example: Puer, quī aquam portat, bonus est. — The boy who carries the water is good.

entries.point: Adverbs: bene, fortiter, celeriter
entries.label: Adverbs
entries.usage: How it is done: -ē and -iter forms, plus irregular bene and male.
entries.example: Mīlitēs fortiter pugnant. — The soldiers fight bravely.

entries.point: Purpose clauses with ut and ne
entries.label: Purpose ut/ne
entries.usage: In-order-to with ut + subjunctive; nē for negative purpose.
entries.example: Puer venit ut puellam videat. — The boy comes to see the girl.

entries.point: Result clauses: tam ... ut
entries.label: Result tam...ut
entries.usage: So X that Y: a signal word, then ut + subjunctive.
entries.example: Rēx tam fortis est ut urbem capiat. — The king is so brave that he captures the city.

entries.point: Cum-clauses: when, since, although
entries.label: cum-clauses
entries.usage: cum + subjunctive covers when, since, and although.
entries.example: Cum rēx dīceret, populus tacēbat. — When the king was speaking, the people were silent.

entries.point: Indirect statement: accusative + infinitive
entries.label: Acc. + infinitive
entries.usage: Reported speech with no 'that': accusative subject, infinitive verb.
entries.example: Sciō rēgem bonum esse. — I know that the king is good.

entries.point: Ablative absolute
entries.label: Ablative absolute
entries.usage: A detached noun + participle pair sets the scene: urbe captā.
entries.example: Urbe captā, mīlitēs vēnērunt. — With the city captured, the soldiers came.

entries.point: Conditionals: the three types of si-clause
entries.label: si-clauses
entries.usage: Real, should-would, and contrary-to-fact conditions with sī.
entries.example: Sī aquam habērem, tibi darem. — If I had water, I would give it to you.

entries.point: Indirect questions and the sequence of tenses
entries.label: Indirect questions
entries.usage: When a question sits inside another sentence — I know what she is saying — and the verb shifts to match.
entries.example: Sciō quid puella dīcat. — I know what the girl is saying.

entries.point: Oratio obliqua: sustained indirect discourse
entries.label: Whole reported speeches
entries.usage: How a historian reports a whole speech without quotation marks: he said that the soldiers had fought.
entries.example: Dīxit rēgem, quī urbem tenēret, bonum esse. — He said that the king, who held the city, was good.

entries.point: Poetic word order: reading real classical lines
entries.label: Poetic order
entries.usage: Reading verse, where poets pull words that belong together apart and the endings put them back.
entries.example: Carpe diem, quam minimum crēdula posterō. — Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow. (Horace, Odes 1.11)

entries.point: Register: Ciceronian period and colloquial Latin
entries.label: Formal vs casual
entries.usage: The long, suspended sentence of a speech against the short, everyday Latin of letters and comedy.
entries.example: Quōusque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā? — How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience? (Cicero, In Catilinam 1)
